title: Option-Based Solving & Exam Strategy
shortDescription: Sometimes the fastest way to solve a question is to stop solving it algebraically and test the options instead — but only when it's actually safe to.
genZNote: The options aren't just the answer menu, they're free hints. Sometimes plugging one in is faster than solving for x at all — just know when that trick backfires.

sections.heading: Core Idea
sections.body: For many multiple-choice Quant questions, deriving the full algebraic solution isn't the only path to the answer — substituting an answer option back into the question, eliminating impossible options, or estimating can be faster. This is a strategy layer that sits on top of every topic above, not a replacement for understanding the underlying method.

sections.heading: The Techniques
bullets: Back-solving / substitution: plug an answer option into the original condition and check if it satisfies it — start with the middle-valued option when options are ordered, since checking it tells you whether to try a bigger or smaller option next.

Elimination: rule out options that violate an obvious constraint (must be even, must be positive, must be a whole number, must be greater than a stated minimum) before testing any of the remaining ones.
Boundary checking: for 'at least / at most' style questions, test the boundary value first — it usually resolves whether the inequality is strict or inclusive.
Estimation: round the numbers and get an approximate answer when the actual options are spread far apart — no need for exact arithmetic if only one option is anywhere near your estimate.
Unit/parity/divisibility checks: if the answer must end in a specific digit, be even/odd, or be divisible by a given number, eliminate every option that fails that single check instantly.

sections.heading: When TO Use Option-Based Solving
bullets: The options are reasonably spread apart (estimation and back-solving are both safe here).
The direct algebraic method involves solving a quadratic, a system of equations, or several steps — substitution of a 'nice' option is often faster.
The question gives a condition that's easy to CHECK against a candidate value, even if it's hard to SOLVE directly (e.g. 'which of these satisfies both conditions').

sections.heading: When NOT to Use It
sections.body: Do not reach for option-based solving when the options are close together in value — small arithmetic slips can make the wrong option look right. Do not use it when checking each option individually would actually take LONGER than solving directly (e.g. a straightforward one-line formula application). Do not use estimation when a question demands an exact figure and the options are close enough that rounding could pick the wrong one.

sections.heading: Common Traps
bullets: Testing options in the order given instead of starting from the middle value when they're ordered — starting in the middle cuts the remaining search space in half with one check.
Forgetting to verify a back-solved option against ALL stated conditions, not just the first one that happens to match.
Using an option-based shortcut on a question that specifically asks 'which of the following is NOT a solution' — read the question direction carefully before eliminating.

sections.heading: Time-Management Strategy for the Full Quant Section
bullets: Identify easy, familiar-pattern questions first and clear them before spending time on anything unfamiliar-looking.
Don't sink excessive time into one stubborn calculation — mark it and move on if a reliable shortcut isn't presenting itself within a reasonable number of attempts.
Use options intelligently on questions where back-solving or elimination is clearly faster than the algebraic route.
Estimate first when exact calculation isn't required to distinguish between well-spread options.
Do a final sanity check on any answer that came from a shortcut — a quick order-of-magnitude or parity check catches a wrong shortcut application before it costs the mark.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Option-based solving uses substitution, elimination, boundary checks, and estimation to reach an answer faster than full algebraic derivation — only when the options are safely spread apart.
keyFacts: Start testing from the MIDDLE option when options are ordered — it halves the remaining search space.
Eliminate options that fail an obvious constraint (parity, sign, divisibility) before testing any in detail.
Estimation is safe only when options are well spread apart; switch to exact calculation when they're close.
commonConfusion: Option-based solving is a speed strategy layered on top of understanding a topic, not a substitute for knowing the underlying method.

highYieldFacts: Testing the middle option first when options are ordered is the single most useful option-based technique.
Parity/divisibility elimination can remove 2–3 options instantly on many Number System and Algebra questions.
commonTraps: Using estimation when options are close together in value.
Testing options in given order instead of starting from the middle when they're ordered.
mustRemember: Option-based solving is only safe when it's actually faster and the options are far enough apart to tolerate small errors.
